title: Keep Users Logged In Across Servers
statement: A ticket site runs four identical servers behind a load balancer. Two requirements are fixed: a user must stay logged in when their next request lands on a different server, and when a user logs out, the logout must take effect on every server at once. Which design meets both requirements best?
examples: User logs in on Server 1, then clicks Buy and the request lands on Server 3
User logs out; a request a second later on Server 2 must be refused
constraints: Four servers now, possibly more at peak
Both requirements must hold, also when a server fails

approaches.name: Sticky sessions: the load balancer always sends a user to the same server, which keeps the session in memory
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.space: Session lives in one server's memory
approaches.why: This avoids the problem instead of meeting it: requests never land on another server. When that server fails, its users lose their sessions and are logged out, which breaks the first requirement.

approaches.name: Store sessions in a shared session store that every server reads
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: About 1 ms to read a session from a nearby store (approximate)
approaches.space: One session record per logged-in user
approaches.why: Any server can read the session, and deleting it logs the user out everywhere at once. The cost is one more component to run and keep available.

approaches.name: A signed token that carries the session, plus a check on every request against a shared list of logged-out tokens
approaches.hint: Token, but with a way to cancel it
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: A signature check plus one lookup per request
approaches.space: The token travels with each request; the list holds only logged-out tokens until they expire
approaches.why: This meets both requirements: any server can check the token, and the shared list makes a logout take effect at once. It is more complex than a session store, so it is a good choice mainly when most requests can skip the store.

approaches.name: A signed token that carries the session, and nothing stored on the servers
approaches.hint: Carry the data with the user
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.space: The token travels with each request
approaches.why: Any server can read the token, but a token that was already issued stays valid until it expires, so a logout cannot take effect at once.

title: Fast and Slow Requests on One Service
statement: A photo service runs four identical servers. Most requests return a small thumbnail in about 20 ms, but about 1 in 20 requests converts a large image and takes about 3 seconds. Users complain that some pages are slow even when the servers are not busy on average. The team wants the simplest change that keeps waiting times even. How should the load balancer choose a server?
examples: Server 2 receives three conversions in a row and has a queue, while Server 4 is idle
constraints: Prefer a change to the load balancer setting only

approaches.name: Round robin: each server in turn
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: Same count per server, very different work
approaches.why: Round robin gives each server the same number of requests, not the same amount of work. It is what the service does now, and slow conversions can still pile up on one server.

approaches.name: Least connections: send each request to the server with the fewest open requests
approaches.hint: Who is least busy right now?
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: New requests avoid servers that are stuck on conversions
approaches.space: One setting on the load balancer
approaches.why: A server busy with a 3-second conversion keeps that connection open, so it receives fewer new requests. It is a single setting, which matches the team's goal.

approaches.name: Send conversions to their own group of servers by path (Layer 7), and thumbnails to another group
approaches.hint: Split the two kinds of work
approaches.label: valid
approaches.space: Two server groups and routing rules to keep up to date
approaches.why: This keeps thumbnails fast even when conversions spike, so it works well. It needs more setup and capacity planning for two groups, so it is not the simplest change asked for.

title: An Internal Tool for 50 People
statement: A company's meeting-room booking tool has 50 users and about 5 requests per second at its busiest. It runs on one small server that is busy about 10% of the time. A few minutes of downtime during a planned restart is acceptable, and a lower cost is better. Next year the company expects 80 users. How should the tool be scaled?
examples: Today: 5 requests per second, server busy 10% of the time
Next year: about 80 ÷ 50 × 5 = 8 requests per second
constraints: Lower cost is preferred, but not at the price of reliability

approaches.name: Keep one server; move to a bigger machine (scale up) only if it gets busy
approaches.hint: Is there a problem to solve yet?
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: About 8 requests per second next year, about 16% busy
approaches.why: Growing from 50 to 80 users raises the load by 80 ÷ 50 = 1.6 times, so the server goes from about 10% to about 16% busy. One server meets every requirement at the lowest cost.

approaches.name: Run two servers behind a load balancer
approaches.label: valid
approaches.space: Two servers and a load balancer
approaches.why: This works and also survives a server failing, but the team accepts short downtime, so it pays for protection it does not need.

approaches.name: Run ten servers in three regions with automatic scaling
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: No real gain at 8 requests per second
approaches.space: Ten servers, balancers and scaling rules
approaches.why: The tool needs a small fraction of one server. This costs many times more and adds parts that can fail, with no benefit at 8 requests per second.
